sentences.text: You have probably heard some version of this at a party, on a podcast, or from a relative who wanted you to keep your day job.
Most new businesses fail, and they fail fast.

onScreenText: Most new businesses fail, and they fail fast.

sentences.text: It sounds like hard-won wisdom. But is it a measurement, or a slogan?

onScreenText: A measurement, or a slogan?

sentences.text: There is a way to check, because the US Bureau of Labor Statistics keeps a table that follows each year's newly opened private-sector establishments and counts how many are still operating, every year after they open.
So let's put the slogan next to the table and see where they part ways.

sentences.text: First, it helps to notice that the slogan comes in more than one size.

Barry's Economics, a channel that pushes back on hustle podcasts, gives the most specific version: "About 25% of businesses fail in their first year. 40% after 3 years, and half of businesses fail after 5 years."

sentences.text: So which is it: a few months, a few years, or a decade?
And does any of it say something about an online store in particular, which is the business most of these videos are actually talking about?
To answer that, we need one group of businesses, followed from the day they open.

sentences.text: In the year that ended in March 2015, 677,876 new private-sector establishments opened in the United States, according to the BLS table.

sentences.text: By March 2018, three years in, 61.4 percent of the class was still open.

From March 2021 on, it never drops below 92.4 percent.
In other words, the danger is front-loaded. A business that makes it through its first couple of years is a much safer bet than one that has just opened.

And ten years on, in March 2025, 235,071 were left out of the original 677,876: 34.7 percent.

sentences.text: So most of the new establishments in this table do close eventually, but most of them are still standing after a few years. And an establishment, in the BLS definition, is typically a single location, like a store or a factory, while a firm may consist of one or more of them.

excerpt.text: The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) consists of a monthly count of employment, quarterly counts of wage levels and business establishments, and a count of workers’ average weekly wages at multiple levels of geographic and industrial detail for use by academic researchers, local governments and other federal agencies, and the public in general. An establishment is commonly understood as a single economic unit, such as a farm, a mine, a factory, or a store, that produces goods or services. Establishments are typically at one physical location and engaged in one, or predominantly one, type of economic activity for which a single industrial classification may be applied. An establishment is in contrast to a firm, or a company, which is a business and may consist of one or more establishments, where each establishment may participate in a different predominant economic activity. The QCEW provides an employment benchmark and sample frames for other U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) programs, as well as a basis of estimation of the wage and salary component for the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis Personal Income statistic. Standard sources used by the QCEW program are the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), for industry detail; Federal Information Processing Standards, for geographic area codes; and the Office of Management and Budget, for size classes.
excerpt.highlight: An establishment is in contrast to a firm, or a company, which is a business and may consist of one or more establishments

sentences.text: A second set of numbers, quoted second-hand, agrees that most close eventually.

Jon Taylor, in a book-length critique of multi-level marketing called The Case against MLM, cites the Small Business Administration as finding that 44 percent of small businesses survive at least four years and 31 percent at least seven.
He also cites a survey by the National Federation of Independent Business in which 64.2 percent of businesses had failed over a 10-year period.

sentences.text: Before you take that curve home, there are limits to what the table can say.
The first is what a closure means. In the BLS definition, a closing is an establishment that reported employment at the end of one quarter and none in the next.

excerpt.text:
What are closings?

These are either establishments with positive third month employment in the previous quarter, with no positive employment reported in the current quarter, or with positive third month employment in the previous quarter followed by zero employment in the current quarter.
excerpt.highlight: with no positive employment reported in the current quarter

citations.label: BLS Business Employment Dynamics FAQ: closings

sentences.text: That records only that the jobs at one location stopped, not why. And because survival is measured location by location, a chain that shuts one branch has a closing in this count, even if the company carries on.

sentences.text: A sale is different. When an establishment changes owners, the BLS links the old record to the new one, so a sale is meant to show up as the same establishment carrying on, not as a closing.

excerpt.text:
How are establishments linked over time?

The linkage process matches establishments' unique State Workforce Agency (SWA) identification numbers (SWA-ID). Between 95 to 97 percent of establishments identified as continuous from quarter to quarter are matched by SWA-ID. The rest are linked in one of three ways. The first method uses predecessor and successor information, identified by the States, which relates records with different SWA-IDs across quarters. Predecessor and successor relations can come about for a variety of reasons, including a change in ownership, a firm restructuring, or a UI account restructuring. If a match cannot be attained in this manner, a probability-based match is used. This match attempts to identify two establishments with different SWA-IDs as continuous. The match is based upon comparisons such as the same name, address, and phone number. Finally, an analyst examines unmatched records individually and forces a match, if possible.

sentences.text: Whether online stores close faster than a bakery or a plumbing firm is a reasonable guess, but it is a guess.
The evidence here cannot tell you how long the typical online store lasts, so the claims about e-commerce stores dying within weeks or months remain unchecked, not confirmed.

sentences.text: First, the honest base rate for a new establishment is not almost certain failure; in this cohort it was a roughly even chance of still operating after five years.
That is sobering, but it is not a reason to dismiss every idea out of hand.
Second, the riskiest single year is the first, when roughly a fifth of these establishments closed; planning to get through it is not a detail.

sentences.text: So, do most new businesses really fail within a few years?
Not in the government's count of new establishments: about half of the class of 2015 was still operating after five years, and a clear majority, 65.3 percent, had gone by ten.

And most online stores within months is a claim this evidence cannot check.
